title: Single Sign-on / Federated Access
description: How single sign-on (Kerberos, Sesame) and federated identity management (trust relationships, SAML, WS-Federation, OpenID, OAuth) let users access many systems with one login.

nodes.title: Allows users to access multiple systems with a single set of credentials
nodes.description:
What single sign-on and federated identity management have in common.
Users love this: they remember one terrible password instead of many, and authenticate once to get access to all their applications.

children.title: Single Sign-on
children.description:
One login gives access to many systems within the same organization.
_____ protocols and systems, such as Kerberos and Sesame, are designed to work within one organization.

children.title: Kerberos
children.description:
A major protocol that enables single sign-on.
Authenticates users with tickets over an insecure network.

children.title: Components
children.description: Kerberos is a complicated, very flexible protocol, so it has many _____: the user, the KDC with its Authentication Service and Ticket Granting Service, the tickets, and the service being accessed.

children.title: User / Client
children.description: The person who wants to access services through Kerberos, and the software on their machine that requests tickets on their behalf.

children.title: Key Distribution Center
children.description:
Contains the two services Kerberos provides: the Authentication Service and the Ticket Granting Service.
It holds the secret keys of all users and services.

children.title: Authentication Service
children.description:
To access a service through Kerberos, the user first authenticates with the Authentication Service.
It checks that the user exists. If so, it sends the user two tickets, one of which is the Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT).

children.title: Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT)
children.description:
Issued by the Authentication Service once the user has authenticated. It proves the user has already logged in.
The user passes the _____ to the Ticket Granting Service, the other component in the KDC, with a couple of messages saying which service the user wants to access.

children.title: Ticket Granting Service
children.description:
Checks that the requested service exists and that the user is authorized to access it.
If so, it creates a Service Ticket and sends it to the user.

children.title: Service Tickets
children.description:
What the user finally sends to the application to get access to it.
The user caches the Service Ticket for future access, while the ticket is valid and not expired.

children.title: Service
children.description: The application the user wants to access. The user presents a Service Ticket to it to get access.

children.title: Symmetric encryption only
children.description:
By default, Kerberos supports only one kind of cryptography: the same secret key encrypts and decrypts.
A significant limitation: quite a few secret keys may need to be created and securely distributed among the components.

children.title: Sesame
children.description:
Another single sign-on protocol, developed in Europe.
Unlike Kerberos, it supports public key (asymmetric) cryptography too.

children.title: Symmetric & Asymmetric encryption
children.description:
Sesame supports both secret key and public key cryptography.
Public key support solves the major problems of secret key cryptography: scalability and key distribution.

children.title: Federated Identity Management (FIM)
children.description:
Access systems across multiple entities.
To the user it looks exactly like single sign-on: enter one set of credentials and get access to many applications.
The key difference: with federated access, users can access not only internal applications, but also externally managed ones, such as SaaS applications in the cloud.

children.title: Trust Relationship
children.description:
Federated access relies on a trust relationship between three entities: the user, the identity provider and the service provider.
The service provider must trust the authentication done by the identity provider before it authorizes the user to access the service.

children.title: Principal / User
children.description: The person who wants to access a service, and whose identity the identity provider vouches for.

children.title: Identity Provider
children.description:
Authenticates the user: verifies who they are by knowledge, ownership or characteristic, then vouches for them to the service.
In many organizations, the _____ is something like Active Directory.

children.title: Relying Party / Service Provider
children.description:
The application the user wants to access. It trusts the identity provider's authentication instead of authenticating the user itself.
Often not owned by the organization, but owned and managed by a vendor. Example: SaaS applications used at work to submit help desk tickets, book travel or enter expenses.

children.title: SAML
children.description:
Several protocols enable federated access. _____ is the major one you need to know.
An open standard that passes authentication and authorization data between an identity provider and a service provider, as XML assertions.
Full name: Security Assertion Markup Language.

children.title: Tokens
children.description: Kerberos sends tickets. SAML does the same thing, but calls them tokens.

children.title: Assertions written in XML
children.description:
What SAML tokens contain: statements such as the user ID, the service ID, and the timestamp and lifetime of the token.
The statements are written in a tag-based markup language, the same family as HTML.

children.title: Components
children.description: SAML was designed for many different use cases, so it is made of several _____ that make it flexible and adaptable: profiles, bindings, protocols and assertions.

children.title: Profiles
children.description: Define how SAML can be used for different business use cases, such as web single sign-on or through LDAP.

children.title: Bindings
children.description: Map SAML onto different communication protocols, such as HTTP, so SAML can communicate across different types of networks.

children.title: Protocol
children.description: Defines how entities send and respond to requests.

children.title: Assertion
children.description: The statements the identity provider makes about the user: authentication, authorization and other attributes.

children.title: WS-Federation
children.description:
A federated access protocol to recognize. Provides both authentication and authorization.
Developed by Microsoft, IBM and others, and used by Active Directory Federation Services (ADFS).

children.title: OpenID
children.description:
A federated access protocol to recognize. Provides authentication.
Lets a user log in to a site with an existing account from another provider, such as a Google account.

children.title: OAuth
children.description:
A federated access protocol to recognize. Provides authorization.
Lets a user grant an application limited access to their resources on another service without sharing their password, for example letting an app read their calendar.
